Transcript: The Cryogenian glaciations. Glacial deposits of this age sit on every craton that preserves rock from the interval, and where the magnetic inclination can be read the ice was grinding bedrock within ten degrees of the equator. A frozen equator leaves nowhere warmer to put the rest of the planet. Sea ice closes over the ocean, evaporation stops, snow stops falling, silicate weathering stops drawing carbon dioxide down, and volcanic gas accumulates until it reaches a few tenths of a bar - several million years of loading, then a deglaciation measured in centuries, then the blanket of carbonate laid straight onto glacial rock at the top of every one of these successions.

Allen, who has worked the Oman sections for thirty years, takes the sealed ocean for a construction of modellers rather than a reading of rock. Inside the diamictites there are graded beds with wave ripples across their tops, sandstones with hummocky cross-stratification, seventeen stacked cycles of coarsening and fining, and lonestones that punched into laminae still soft enough to bend around them. Waves need open water. Debris rained onto the sea floor from floating ice needs ice that is melting. Sand delivered in graded pulses needs rivers, and rivers need rain.

Another reading has the planet tipped over. An obliquity past fifty-four degrees makes the tropics the coldest ground on Earth, and equatorial glaciers follow from the geometry alone.

Tillites of this age turn up at every paleolatitude the method resolves. The Port Askaig beds were laid down near forty degrees. Australian and Namibian units sit higher again. The Congo craton's span both ends of the range inside a single formation.

Iron formation returns in these successions after an absence of a billion and a half years. Loading deep water with dissolved iron on that scale takes an ocean shut away from the air. The iron units are lenses: metres thick, a few kilometres across, sitting between glacial members and passing sideways into ordinary glaciomarine mud.

Ash beds above and below the Sturtian give it fifty-seven million years. Sections in Oman, Scotland, Namibia and South Australia, tied to one another by those ashes, carry the same architecture through the whole of that interval: diamictite, a wave-worked top, graded sandstone, diamictite again, a dozen times over and more.
prompt: [Academic Talk - Earth Science] Given the evidence the talk sets out, which claim about the Cryogenian ocean is left standing, and in whose version?
choices: That the ocean froze over from pole to pole and stayed shut for millions of years, the carbon dioxide loading and the carbonate blanket at the top of each succession following from that closure.
That equatorial ice calls for no global freeze at all, a tilt past fifty-four degrees making the tropics the coldest ground on the planet and putting glaciers there by geometry.
That open water and a working water cycle ran through the glaciation, as Allen reads the Oman rock, with ice grinding bedrock near the equator all the same.
That the diamictites are debris flows and storm beds of ordinary marine origin, the glaciation being a construction laid over rock that never called for one, which is Allen's position.
correct_answer: That open water and a working water cycle ran through the glaciation, as Allen reads the Oman rock, with ice grinding bedrock near the equator all the same.
explanation: C2 rather than C1 because the talk never grades the three positions and never states a conclusion: the opening account is delivered warmly and without hedging, and a listener who takes that warmth as endorsement answers A, the sealed-ocean story, which the closing correlation contradicts by putting wave-worked tops and graded sandstone through the entire fifty-seven-million-year interval on four cratons. The paleolatitude survey disposes of B by entailment rather than by denial, and D fails because the same closing paragraph, plus the equatorial inclinations of the opening, keeps the glaciation itself global and long. What is left is the narrowed form of the objection, and nothing in the talk says whose it is.

prompt: [Academic Talk - Earth Science] The iron formation paragraph sits between the paleolatitude survey and the ash-bed correlation with no connective to either. What work is it doing?
choices: It grants the shut-off ocean the opening account requires and then bounds it, the iron bodies being lenses that pass sideways into ordinary glacial mud.
It supplies the independent confirmation that the ocean lay sealed beneath ice for the millions of years the carbon dioxide loading requires, iron of that kind forming under no other conditions.
It fixes the age of the glaciation by tying these successions to the older iron formations that preceded them by a billion and a half years.
It identifies iron formation as the deposit reliable enough to recognise a Cryogenian succession wherever the paleomagnetic signal has been overprinted.
correct_answer: It grants the shut-off ocean the opening account requires and then bounds it, the iron bodies being lenses that pass sideways into ordinary glacial mud.
explanation: C2 rather than C1 because the paragraph is three bare declaratives whose force turns entirely on the last clause: the return of iron formation reads as a gift to the opening account, and a listener tracking who is speaking stops there and takes B. The geometry is what carries the argument - metres thick, kilometres across, passing sideways into ordinary glaciomarine mud - so the shut-off condition is granted and then confined to patches, which is the same restriction the closing correlation makes in time. Nothing in the talk marks the shift, and neither C nor D is denied anywhere; they simply do not follow from what the sentences say.

Transcript: The price of the human brain. Two per cent of body mass and a fifth of the resting energy budget: brain is among the costliest tissue a mammal carries. A human at rest burns what Kleiber's line predicts for a mammal of the mass, and no more. An organ trebled in size within two million years, with the total holding steady, means a draw of the same order was closed off somewhere else, and the gut is where the money was found. Human digestive tissue runs some forty per cent under the mass expected for a primate of that size, gram for gram it costs about what brain tissue costs, and marrow, meat and cooked starch are what make a shortened gut workable.

Navarrete weighed the organs out of a hundred and ninety-one species, carcasses from zoos, from museums, from roadsides. Brain mass against digestive-tract mass, body size held constant, gives a cloud with no slope in it. The variable that does run against brain mass, across rodents, bats, carnivores and primates alike, is stored fat: within each order the fattest species carry the smallest brains for their size. Where the ledger balances, on this evidence, it balances against adipose and against the cost of hauling a heavy body about.

There are people who take the ledger itself for the error, throughput being something a lineage can enlarge as readily as it can redistribute.

The elephantnose fish runs a brain that takes three fifths of the oxygen its whole body consumes. Its gut is the length a fish of its habits usually has, and its fat stores are the usual size for one. A dedicated vascular network off the swimbladder feeds the enlarged cerebellum, and the animal keeps to the shallowest, best-aerated water it can reach.

Doubly labelled water, on three hundred and some humans and on chimpanzees, gorillas and orangutans handled the same way, puts human daily expenditure four hundred kilocalories above the chimpanzee figure at matched fat-free mass. The gorillas come next, then the orangutans, and the order across the four species is the order of their brain sizes.

Body fat, measured by isotope dilution in those same subjects, comes out at two to three times the chimpanzee fraction in the humans, and the human infants in the sample carry more of it than any other primate that has been weighed.
prompt: [Academic Talk - Human Evolution] By the end of the talk, which account of how the brain's cost was met is still consistent with the measurements reported?
choices: That the gut was cut to pay for the brain, the shortened human digestive tract and the improved diet that makes it workable being the transaction that funded encephalisation.
That the payment came out of stored fat rather than out of the gut, the way it does across rodents, bats, carnivores and primates alike.
That brain tissue in the human line grew cheaper to run gram for gram, which is why the resting budget stayed on the line Kleiber drew.
That the total was raised rather than reapportioned, an organ-against-organ ledger holding only for a lineage whose daily budget stays where it is.
correct_answer: That the total was raised rather than reapportioned, an organ-against-organ ledger holding only for a lineage whose daily budget stays where it is.
explanation: C2 rather than C1 because the surviving position is the one nobody in the talk argues for: it is reported in a single unhedged clause and then dropped, while the two positions that are developed at length are each undone by a later measurement. A listener backing the speaker takes A, but the expenditure figures show the daily total rising with brain size across the four apes, which is the premise the gut trade-off needs held fixed. B is the more inviting trap because it is the last argued position stated, and the closing sentence undoes it by pairing the largest brain with the largest fat fraction. C is never raised and does not follow from the resting figure, which is reported as ordinary rather than as low.

choices: It puts an upper bound on what a brain can cost, three fifths of an animal's oxygen being the highest fraction any lineage has been found to reach.
It shows an expensive brain carried without a compensating reduction anywhere, the cost met by enlarging and routing the supply instead of by trimming another organ.
It identifies oxygen rather than calories as the currency brain tissue is really paid for in, which is why ledgers built on organ mass give a cloud with no slope.
It supplies a case in which diet quality did the work, the habitat allowing the fish to feed well enough that no organ had to be shortened for it.
correct_answer: It shows an expensive brain carried without a compensating reduction anywhere, the cost met by enlarging and routing the supply instead of by trimming another organ.
explanation: C2 rather than C1 because the paragraph reads at first as a display of how expensive brains can get, which is the opening account's own premise, and that reading takes A. The load is carried by the two flat clauses in the middle - the gut ordinary, the fat stores ordinary - which remove both candidate offsets at once, and by the vascular network and the choice of well-aerated water, which say where the cost went instead. Getting it requires seeing that the example is a dissociation rather than an illustration, and that it stands next to the one position in the talk that nobody defends. C mistakes a detail of the fish for a claim about the mammal data; D is a rearrangement of the opening account's diet clause, which the paragraph gives no support for.
